edits.find: The Western Cape should apply the same test to its own record: growth counts when deliberate change drives it, not when recovery returns lost visitors (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p8).
edits.repl: The Western Cape should apply the same test to its own record: growth counts when deliberate change drives it, not when recovery returns lost visitors (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p8). The province has its own precedent above the 5% mark. International two-way passengers at Cape Town International rose from 1.71 million in 2015 to 3.1 million in 2024, about 6.8% a year (Cape Town Air Access, Letsema Update, Nov 2025, slide 4, computed). Most of the rise came before COVID: traffic grew about 11% a year from 2015 to 2019 and about 3.5% a year from 2019 to 2024, inside the norm (Cape Town Air Access, Letsema Update, Nov 2025, slide 4, computed). Over the decade the Cape Town Air Access partnership, formed in 2015, counts 33 new routes, regional services among them, against the 17 mainline services in the peer comparison above (Cape Town Air Access, Letsema Update, Nov 2025, slide 1, slide 5).
edits.reason: Assessment 5, Chapter 2, 2.1 (Medium): a home precedent for growth above 5%. Factbase: CTIA international two-way passengers 1.71m (2015), 2.61m (2019), 3.1m (2024); 52% rise 2015 to 2019 and 18% 2019 to 2024 (Letsema Update slide 4); partnership initiated 2015 (slide 1); 33 new routes since inception, regional points such as Maun and Walvis Bay among them (slides 2, 5). Computed: 6.8% a year over 2015 to 2024; about 11% a year over 2015 to 2019 and about 3.5% over 2019 to 2024, which applies the 2.1 test (the post-2019 rate sits inside the 3% to 5% norm). Review: the 33 is set against the 17 mainline services of [18].

edits.repl: No case of failure was studied (Inception Report, Nov 2025, p16; the plan asked for four success cases and two that underperformed). The nearest local record is the City's own. That is a plan, not a destination, so the gap remains.

blocks.text: The province converts a small share of a large market

Global demand is not the constraint. Over 2022 to 2024 the province received 3.6 million international arrivals in total, about 1.2 million a year (Wesgro Research, Tourism Source Market Analysis, Nov 2025, p2, computed). That is about 0.1% of global tourist arrivals over the period and 0.05% of global tourist spend (Wesgro Research, Tourism Source Market Analysis, Nov 2025, p2).

blocks.source: Wesgro Research, Tourism Source Market Analysis, Nov 2025, p4 (air outbound trips, arrivals and shares). Last column computed: Western Cape arrivals as a share of South Africa's arrivals from the same market.

blocks.text: Most Indian and Chinese visitors to South Africa never reach the province. About 27% of South Africa's Indian arrivals and 29% of its Chinese arrivals came to the Western Cape over the three years, against 52% to 58% for the UK, Germany, France and the Netherlands (Wesgro Research, Tourism Source Market Analysis, Nov 2025, p3, p4, computed). Those visitors are already in the country, so they are a market to win alongside new routes. South Africa also competes as an African choice more than a global one. Americans ranked it second in Africa but 52nd to 57th worldwide over 2022 to 2024, and Chinese travellers 53rd to 69th (Wesgro Research, Tourism Source Market Analysis, Nov 2025, p5 to p6).

The model splits markets differently from SA Tourism. For the UK and Germany its 2025 starting points sit within about 1% of SA Tourism's yearly average for 2022 to 2024. For India and China with Hong Kong they are about four and five times it, 76,547 and 43,412 against about 19,300 and 8,900. The Netherlands' is about 1.8 times SA Tourism's and France's about a third (Wesgro Research, Tourism Source Market Analysis, Nov 2025, p3, p4, computed; Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p21, p22). The hub-traveller counts later in this section are a third series again. Section 1.1 records the open item on what the model counts.

edits.reason: Assessment 5, Chapter 2, 2.2 (High): capture by market on air outbound trips, as the short table the assessment proposes (TSMA p4, three-year totals, labelled; decisions: market capture). SA Tourism yearly averages, 2022 to 2024 (TSMA p3, p4, three-year totals divided by three): UK 184,344, Germany 131,106, Netherlands 61,263, France 59,326, India 19,325, China with Hong Kong 8,887; model 2025 points UK 182,398, Germany 130,475 (within about 1%), Netherlands 107,938 (about 1.8 times), France 21,495 (about a third) on MA p21, India 76,547 and China 43,412 (about four and five times) on MA p22. The gap runs both ways, so it is a split of markets, not a different measure; pointed to the open item in 1.1. Decisions: 3.6m is a three-year total, about 1.2m a year. Review (length): the capture paragraph no longer repeats the shares the table prints.

blocks.text: Domestic demand gives the province no cushion. The province recorded 3.458 million domestic trips in 2024, 6.1% fewer than at the start of 2020 (Provincial Economic Review and Outlook 2025, p69 to p70). Provinces such as the Eastern Cape drew more of the budget-conscious recovery (Provincial Economic Review and Outlook 2025, p69 to p70). The mandate here is international, but growth that lifts peak prices could crowd out the domestic visitors on whom the green season and the regions lean. The action plan should therefore track domestic trips as context.

edits.reason: Assessment 5, Chapter 2, 2.2 (Medium): one paragraph on domestic demand; assessment 6, fourth finding (domestic trips fell as prices rose; international growth can price out domestic visitors). PERO pp69 to 70 (municipal factbase). Kept to one paragraph as the assessment advises, since the mandate is international; review (length): the Blueprint aside is dropped.

edits.find: Growth to 2.5 million is therefore a supply programme before it is a marketing one.
edits.repl: Wesgro's FY26 to FY30 plan asks for faster growth still. Its target of 800,000 to 1 million new international arrivals over five years is 2.6 to 3.3 times the base case's gain to 2030 and about twice the accelerated case's (Wesgro, Strategic Plan 2025/26 to 2029/30, p20, computed; Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p19, p20; section 1.1). blocks.text: Cape Town's cruise berth has room, and port spending is not going to cruise. In 2024/25 the berth handled 83 calls against a season capacity of 150 or more, with about 127,000 passengers (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p110; Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p37; that source counts 79 vessels for the season, while passengers agree; the Infrastructure Report also prints about 40% use of the season, on a basis it does not state). Its limits are a 300m ship length, the South-Easter wind and no shore power (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p110 to p112). Wesgro's plan targets 250 calls over FY26 to FY30, about 50 a year (Wesgro, Strategic Plan 2025/26 to 2029/30, p20).

Cruise value comes from the mix of passengers, not their number. International passengers rose from 55,495 in 2022/23 to 100,255 in 2024/25, about 81% more (StratEcon, Cruise Liner Economic Contribution Study 2024/25, Oct 2025, p9 to p10, computed). Total passengers fell about 12% over the same three seasons (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p37, computed). Section 1.2 sets out what the season added to provincial GDP-R and jobs. The base is volatile. In 2023/24, 20 of the 67 calls were ships rerouted by the Middle East conflict. Wesgro's 50 rounds up an average of 47 that leaves them out, so the target sits below the 79 vessels of 2024/25 (Wesgro, Strategic Plan 2025/26 to 2029/30, p20; Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p37).

Decisions, 250 cruise calls: a five-year total, about 50 a year, from a 47-call average (67 less 20 reroutes, plan p20), so the target sits below 2024/25's 79 vessels (Diag p37; assessment 6, first finding). Decisions, cruise value: international passengers 55,495 to 100,255 (StratEcon pp9 to 10); total fell about 12% (144,125 to 127,178, Diag p37, computed). Assessment 6, third finding.

blocks.text: The province already holds instruments for that escalation. Its own visa study, by BDO for the Department of Economic Development, ranks the reforms to press for: published processing times first, then visa exemption for China, India and Nigeria (BDO for DEDAT, Western Cape Visa Regime Study, Jul 2024, p34). Wesgro's Advocacy and Advisory unit exists to press such evidence on the levers the province does not control (section 1.2). The Tourism Blueprint 2030 already names the same barriers: poor continental air access from restricted markets, a costly and inconvenient visa regime and persistent safety concerns (Tourism Blueprint 2030, p4, p11).

blocks.text: Transport and safety plans already exist

Two plans already reach into the visitor's journey. The Department of Mobility's draft Provincial Land Transport Framework includes a Tourism Transport Strategy, which plans to revive the MyCiTi airport service with ACSA and to sign and maintain tourist routes (Western Cape Department of Mobility, draft Provincial Land Transport Framework, Apr 2025, ch12). The City has designed its own Tourist Safety Programme. It sets out secure zones in higher-risk tourism areas, a Tourist Police unit, victim support and safety forums (City of Cape Town, Tourism Development Framework 2019 to 2024, p5). The action plan should build on both plans rather than start new ones. [Open item: the City of Cape Town and the Department of Mobility to confirm which parts of these plans are adopted, funded or running.]
